title: Artificial Intelligence and State Insurance Regulation (Issue Brief)
date_evidence: March 2026 Artificial Intelligence and State Insurance Regulation
key_claim: State regulators, through the NAIC, supervise insurers' use of AI in underwriting, pricing, claims and fraud detection under existing statutory authority; the NAIC adopted AI Principles in 2020 and a Model Bulletin in 2023 clarifying that existing insurance laws apply to AI systems, and regulators are piloting an AI systems evaluation tool. AI 'does not alter insurers' legal obligations'.
verbatim_quote: It does not alter insurers’ legal obligations.
notes: NAIC Government Affairs issue brief, title page dated March 2026. Verified via WebFetch of the PDF; full text read. Used for the regulatory-context framing (who supervises insurer conduct on AI).

title: Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group — 2026 Spring National Meeting materials
date_evidence: Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group Tuesday, March 24, 2026 11:30 AM - 12:30 PM
key_claim: The NAIC's AI Systems Evaluation Tool entered a multi-state pilot in 2026 (11 pilot states as of the Feb. 17 2026 meeting, after Maryland and Louisiana joined); the Working Group intends to finalise the tool for adoption consideration at the Fall National Meeting, and presented guidance on operationalising the NAIC AI Model Bulletin including an AI risk taxonomy of harm, model cards, model-drift validation and protected-class bias testing.
notes: NAIC Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group meeting packet, 2026 Spring National Meeting, dated 3/24/26. Verified via WebFetch of the PDF; full text read. Used for the regulator-tooling pathway point.

publisher: arXiv (Leung, Zhang, Ling, Toyoda and Loh)
title: The Insurability Frontier of AI Risk: Mapping Threats to Affirmative Coverage, Silent Exposures, and Exclusions
key_claim: Coding 55 AI threat classes against 26 insurance products, endorsements and exclusion regimes identifies a four-tier insurability frontier: affirmatively insured perils, silent-AI exposures under legacy lines, actively excluded perils, and perils outside conventional private insurance. Affirmative AI cover is differentiating by carrier (Munich Re around model performance/drift; Armilla and the Lloyd's market around hallucination; Tokio Marine Kiln and CFC around IP/E&O; Coalition around deepfake). Foundation-model concentration is the clearest genuinely novel insurability frontier because upstream model failure can correlate losses across many cedents at once.
verbatim_quote: foundation model concentration is the clearest genuinely novel insurability frontier
notes: arXiv preprint 2605.18784 (q-fin.RM), primary empirical coding study, arXiv-issued DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2605.18784. Classified Tier 2 (academic preprint on a recognised repository). Verified via WebFetch of the abstract page.

publisher: Tufts Now (Josephine Wolff, The Fletcher School, Tufts University)
title: Can Companies Insure Against AI's Growing Risks?
key_claim: AI lawsuits and settlements are proliferating (Anthropic agreed a USD 1.5 billion copyright settlement in 2025; a Florida jury found Tesla partially liable for an Autopilot crash, awarding over USD 240 million); the largest AI companies cannot buy as much insurance as they want and some are considering self-insuring with investor funds; insurers lack reliable data to price AI losses and fear costs could be exceedingly high; many existing cyber and commercial general liability policies already cover AI-related risks, and the challenge parallels the early evolution of cyber insurance.
notes: Analysis by Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School, Tufts; published on Tufts Now (university institution), originally on Econofact. Classified Tier 2 (academic institution / named expert analysis). Verified via WebFetch; full text read. Also a counter-argument source (existing coverage; cyber parallel).

publisher: Mark A. Geistfeld, Connecticut Insurance Law Journal (UConn)
title: Insurability and Liability for AI-Caused Harms
key_claim: Insurability and liability are structurally interdependent: liability rules for AI-caused harms cannot be set without accounting for how they change the cost and feasibility of insuring against injury. Expanding liability (e.g. strict enterprise liability) substantially increases total insurance cost through duplicated coverage, and can disadvantage the very right-holders the rule is meant to protect. Accounting for the structural relation between insurability and liability is essential for efficient and fair liability rules governing AI-caused harms.
notes: Law-review article by Mark A. Geistfeld (NYU School of Law), Connecticut Insurance Law Journal (2026), hosted on UConn Digital Commons; online date 6 May 2026. Classified Tier 2 (academic). Verified via WebFetch of the abstract/landing page. Used for the Implications structural-framing and Counter-Argument.

title: AI Exclusions in Insurance Policies: Broad Language, Uncertain Impact
key_claim: Carriers such as Berkley have introduced 'absolute' AI exclusions in D&O, E&O and fiduciary liability policies barring claims 'based upon, arising out of, or attributable to' any actual or alleged use, deployment or development of AI, with an extremely broad definition of AI; the Insurance Services Office (ISO) introduced three AI-related endorsements (CG 40 47, CG 40 48 and CG 35 08) for commercial general liability; but courts construe exclusions narrowly and against the insurer, and an exclusion may not be read so broadly that it 'swallows' coverage and renders it illusory.
verbatim_quote: based upon, arising out of, or attributable to
notes: Insurance-recovery analysis by Jay Konkel and Hadhy Ayaz, Pillsbury (policyholder-side law firm). Tier 3 (legal trade analysis). Verified via WebFetch; full text read. Quotes Berkley exclusion language verbatim and the ISO endorsement set.

title: Viewpoint: AI Insurance Is Not Cyber Insurance With Extra Steps
key_claim: AI claims are not landing as breaches or ransomware but as ordinary chatbot, call-analytics and consultation interactions; early cases (Valencia v. Invoca, applying California's CIPA 'mere capability' standard; Lisota v. Heartland Dental) show an AI claim 'simply arrives looking for a home' across cyber, technology E&O, privacy, media, professional liability, regulatory defence or management liability, so treating AI risk as cyber risk in a new costume is a category error.
verbatim_quote: The claim simply arrives looking for a home.
notes: Viewpoint by Peter Hawley (insurance strategist, former international head of cyber at Everest), republished from LinkedIn in Insurance Journal. Tier 3 (quality trade press; named practitioner viewpoint). Verified via WebFetch; full text read.

title: Are AI exclusions in D&O becoming inevitable?
key_claim: Gallagher executives report that D&O insurers are taking a wait-and-see approach because AI is too poorly understood to rewrite policy language aggressively, but expect AI exclusions to be added much as they were for cyber, on the logic that 'policies can't remain silent forever'; the current D&O concern is 'AI-washing' (overstated AI disclosures); public-company D&O pricing rose roughly 1% in Q1 2026 after years of declines.
notes: Trade journalism, Insurance Business (KM Business Information). Tier 3. Verified via WebFetch; full text read. Used as nuance / partial counter-evidence (insurers not yet imposing broad D&O exclusions) and for the cyber-parallel framing.
